# What computational biology actually is

How would you find out whether a gene you've never heard of exists in an animal
nobody has sequenced?

You can't look it up. Nothing from that animal has ever been deposited
anywhere, so no database holds a record for it, and no amount of clicking will
produce one. What you can do is take the gene from a relative somebody did
sequence, then ask how far across the tree of life that gene reaches. If it
turns up in a mouse and in a chicken, an unsequenced mammal is a good bet. If
it turns up in nothing but chimpanzees, it isn't. You'll run that comparison
across five species in Chapter 19.

So the answer is a comparison, and what you compare against is the pile of
sequence everybody else has already deposited. This book ran one of those
comparisons on 2 August 2026. The database it searched held 128,547,243
sequences, with 948,086,538,397 letters between them.

## Nobody can read the pile

GenBank Release 3 came out in December 1982 and held 680,338 bases in 606
records. Print that at 60 letters to a line and 50 lines to a page, so 3,000
letters a page, and the entire database is a 227-page paperback. You could have
held all of it in one hand.

<!-- nlr-allow: 3000 -->

NCBI's release notes carry a table of every release since. The last row is
Release 272. It's counted the same way as the 1982 one: 79,604,775,262 bases in
192,425,204 records. At that same page size the printout runs past 26 million
pages.

That table isn't the whole database. It leaves out the records that arrive as
whole projects instead of one gene at a time. The release notes count those on
a line of their own: another 50,068,290,456,326 bases of whole-genome and
transcriptome sets. Nobody typed those in one at a time either.

::: {.asof}
Every GenBank number here came from NCBI's release notes on 2 August 2026, at
Release 272. Whatever the totals say when you go and look, they'll be bigger.
:::

The rate matters more than the total. NCBI prints one sentence above that
table: from 1982 to now, the number of bases in GenBank has doubled about every
18 months. The last few rows have gone flat, because the bulk arrivals land on
the whole-genome line instead. The pile still outruns you. Your reading speed
has not doubled once.

::: {.why}
The field exists because of a mismatch between two rates. A sequencing machine
writes bases far faster than a person reads them, and the machines get faster
every few years while people don't. That gap is why these tools exist at all.
Every technique in this book is a way of putting a question to a pile you'll
never look at directly.
:::

## Three questions a microscope can't answer

You'll produce all three of these answers yourself before the book is done.

**A 649-base fragment of DNA is sitting in a file with nothing attached saying
where it came from. What animal is it?**

*Gadus chalcogrammus*, the Alaska pollock. Its best match in the database is a
record called AB182303, at 100 percent identity across the whole fragment, with
a bit score of 1199.6. You run that search yourself in Chapter 6, and Chapter 7
says what those two numbers are worth. Notice the shape of the work. A species
name came out of a plain text file, by comparing that file against the whole
database.

**Human *BRCA1* and mouse *Brca1* are the same gene in two animals. Are the
proteins the same size?**

Nearly. The human protein is 1,863 amino acids and the mouse protein is 1,812,
so 51 residues apart. The genes are nowhere near as close. The human gene
occupies 126,033 bases of chromosome 17 and the mouse gene occupies 63,222
bases of chromosome 11. Half the gene went missing. The protein barely moved.
Chapter 5 has you read all four numbers off the database yourself, and no
microscope ever built reports a residue count.

**When a mouse starts producing milk, what happens to *Brca1* in the basal
cells of her mammary gland?**

It collapses. The gene reads 8.3 counts per million in virgin animals and 0.9
in lactating ones. In the luminal cells it hardly shifts, 20.5 down to 19.3, on
a unit that Chapter 20 defines. Getting there means holding 27,179 genes across
12 samples in one table and comparing groups of columns. The same table answers
the same question for every other gene in it. That's Part 4 of this book, on
that exact dataset.

## Three names for this, and why you shouldn't pick one

People use three words for this work, and the words do mean different things.

[Bioinformatics]{.term def="Building the software and databases that store
biological data and hand it back."} is building and running the tools and the
databases that hold biological data. The output is a resource other people use:
BLAST is bioinformatics, and so is the collection it searches.

[Computational biology]{.term def="Using computation to answer a biological
question, rather than to build a tool."} is using computation to answer a
question about biology. The output is an answer: this gene drops during
lactation, these two species split in that order.

[Systems biology]{.term def="The study of how genes and proteins behave in
groups, rather than one gene at a time."} is the study of what the parts do
together instead of what one gene does alone. Genes act on each other, and a
network of them can behave in ways you can't recover from any single member.

Here's the part nobody tells you, and you can check it yourself. Open any job
board and search all three words. Every time I've done that, the same duties
come back under all three headings. The word in the title tracks which
department is hiring, not what you'd do all day. So don't pick a label and
study toward it. The skill under all three names is one skill: getting a
defensible answer out of data you didn't generate.

None of that tells you what the work feels like from the inside, so here's an
ordinary Tuesday.

::: {.notebox label="A Tuesday"}
You open yesterday's notebook and it won't run. It ran yesterday because you'd
clicked the cells in an order you can no longer reconstruct. That's the first
hour.

Then you go to attach gene names to your results and find the two files speak
different languages. GSE60450, the dataset in Part 4, ships NCBI Entrez Gene
IDs and no symbols at all. Converting 27,179 of them is the rest of the
morning, and fiddly work like that takes longer than hard work does.

After lunch you plot something and it looks wrong in a way you can't name. The
counts in that dataset run basal samples first and then luminal ones. The
accession list at GEO runs the other way. Line them up by position, as anyone
would, and all 12 samples carry the wrong label. Nothing errors. The plot is
well-labeled and backwards.

The stretch where you learn something about biology is the short part of the
day. It's worthless unless the file wrangling was right, which is why the file
wrangling gets the hours.
:::

Chapter 3 lays out how the rest of these chapters are built, and what each box
on the page is for. Chapter 4 gets you somewhere to run code.
